entry.title: ACH Return Codes Demystified: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each
entry.summary: ACH Return Codes Demystified: R01 to R85 and How to Handle Each When an ACH payment fails, the originating financial institution receives a return code. Understanding what each code means—and how to respond—is critical for any developer building payment infrastructure. Unlike generic error messages, ACH return codes follow the NACHA (National Automated Clearing House Association) standard and map to specific, actionable failure reasons. ACH transfers are not instantaneous. A payout initiated today may settle in 1–2 business days, and returns can arrive days or even weeks later. If your system doesn't decode and act on return codes, you'll miss critical signals: Is the account closed? Did the customer dispute the charge? Is there insufficient funding? There is no single correct interval. What keeps a site both patched and working is a fixed cadence, a fixed order of operations, and a rollback you have already tested. Here is the schedule I would put on a calendar, and exactly what happens inside the maintenance window.

Anything whose changelog says security fix within 24-72 hours production, straight after a backup
Routine plugin updates once a month, same day, same hour staging first, then production
Plugins that touch money (payments, checkout, tax, shipping) once a month, staging plus a test order staging first, always
Major version bumps (the first number changes) once a quarter, batched staging, changelog read line by line

entry.title: Designing an AI general ledger: the model proposes, deterministic code disposes
entry.summary:
An AI general ledger works when the model only produces proposals (a category, a match, a question with a confidence) and deterministic code validates, applies, logs and can reverse them. Every balance and total comes from the ledger, never the model. That is how ZeraBooks is built. This post sketches that shape in TypeScript. It illustrates the design; it isn't our source code. I'm on the ZeraBooks team. When people hear "AI does the bookkeeping" they picture a model writing journal entries. That's the design we avoided. The model never writes to the ledger and never does arithmetic. It returns a small structured proposal, and everything after that is ordinary code with tests. type Confidence = "sure" | "fairly_sure" | "not_sure";

entry.title: WordPress forms to a CRM over webhook: persist first, retry with backoff, dedupe on replay
entry.summary: The failure is always the same shape. The visitor presses submit, PHP makes one wp_remote_post() call, the CRM answers 502 or the connection hangs until the request is killed, and the lead exists nowhere. The visitor saw a thank-you message. Nobody follows up. This is the version I would ship: write the lead into a queue table inside WordPress first, then let a worker deliver it with backoff, an idempotency key, and a dead-letter state that a human is forced to look at. Everything below is one must-use plugin. The outbound request blocks the visitor. The default timeout is generous, the form looks frozen, and people press submit again. A retryable error is treated as success. 429, 500, 502, 503 and connection timeouts are the normal case, not the exception. A permanent error is invisible. …
